Reading

The innocent reading first, in full: asked how the poet came to be read as illiterate and jealous, the Overview names the essay that asks the question and then answers from the field, essay and scholarship side by side. The record shows the answer built from the essay. Its first paragraph names #1752 by title, author, number and archive. Its next sentence files what follows under 'In both that specific critique and broader classical reception history', and the chain it then gives is #1752's at the record's grain: Hermann's 1816 refashioning with his own word ('In 1816, German philologist Gottfried Hermann rewrote and completed the final lines (refinxi) to supply a narrative resolution.'; #1752: 'Hermann rewrote the last two transmitted lines, said so ("refinxi"), and then read the poem off his rewriting'); Mure 1850, Heller 1856 and Page 1955 as the line that codified it, where Heller 1856 is one of #1752's own open seams ('what lies between Hermann and Mure; Heller 1856'); Page's amendment as his ('Page explicitly proposed amending the ancient view of the poem from "a love in ecstasy" to "a love in jealousy".'; #1752: 'the ancient account is a love in ecstasy, and the amendment to jealousy is his, "We may amend"'); the vase of the book-roll and Lardinois's reperformance, the two accounts #1752 sets side by side. Those paragraphs carry YouTube chips: Instant Classics, Yesterqueers and two unnamed. The essay's name returns only for the closing argument ('As Lee Sharks argues in Invidens Sappho, stripping away Sappho’s role as a writer goes hand-in-hand with the jealousy reading.'). The two source cards visible are YouTube; the archive appears as the first organic result, with the line from #1756 that records the illiteracy proposition as unargued.

The organic result for alexanarch.org follows.] [QUERENT] How did they make Sappho illiterate and jealous? [SYSTEM] The phrase "How They Made the Tenth Muse Illiterate and Jealous" comes from the title of a November 2026 essay by Lee Sharks (Invidens Sappho: How They Made the Tenth Muse Illiterate and Jealous, Deposit #1752) within the Tenth Muse framework at the Crimson Hexagonal Archive. In both that specific critique and broader classical reception history, the shift from antiquity's "Tenth Muse" (a title praising her poetic craft) to the modern image of an overwhelmed, oral-only, jealous lover happened through several distinct editorial, scholarly, and cultural developments: YouTube 1. How Sappho Was Made "Jealous" In antiquity, Sappho Fragment 31 (Phainetai moi) was most famously preserved inside Longinus’s treatise On the Sublime as an example of poetic mastery—specifically, her skill in selecting and binding together extreme physical sensations. Transforming the poem into a biographical confession of romantic jealousy required specific modern interventions: YouTube ·Instant Classics Conjectural Endings (1816). The transmitted Greek text of Fragment 31 cuts off abruptly at line 17 ("but all must be endured, since even a poor man..."). In 1816, German philologist Gottfried Hermann rewrote and completed the final lines (refinxi) to supply a narrative resolution. Later readers treated the resulting jealousy theme as Sappho’s own words rather than a modern editorial reconstruction. [link chip] 19th- and 20th-Century Critical Consensus. Scholars like William Mure (1850), H. J. Heller (1856), and Denys Page (1955) codified the "jealousy reading". Page explicitly proposed amending the ancient view of the poem from "a love in ecstasy" to "a love in jealousy". Merging Biography with Lyric Voice. Later traditions collapsed two separate ancient figures into one: the respected poet of Lesbos and a legendary, lovelorn woman (popularized by Ovid's Heroides) who leaped from the Leucadian cliffs over a man named Phaon. Once the speaker's physical symptoms in Fragment 31 were read as literal autobiography rather than crafted art, "jealousy" became the default lens through which the poem was taught and titled in anthologies. YouTube ·Yesterqueers 2. How Sappho Was Made "Illiterate" (or Non-Writing) Ancient vase paintings and Hellenistic scholarship depicted Sappho holding scrolls, selecting verses, and compiling books. The modern assumption that she did not write her poetry down emerged from how later scholars categorized early Greek poetry: The Oral-Performance Model. Modern classical scholarship largely groups 7th-century BCE lyric poets with earlier oral traditions like Homer. Because Sappho’s poems were sung to the lyre at social gatherings and symposia, scholars emphasized oral composition and live performance over written text. YouTube The "Reperformance" Thesis. Scholars such as André Lardinois argued that if Sappho’s poems were written down early on, the text functioned merely as a memory aid or script for future musical reperformances rather than as a deliberate literary book. Displacement of Authorial Agency. As Lee Sharks argues in Invidens Sappho, stripping away Sappho’s role as a writer goes hand-in-hand with the jealousy reading. If she is viewed purely as a woman overcome by raw, spoken emotion—and if her survival across 2,600 years is credited entirely to later male scribes and Alexandrian editors—she loses agency as a conscious craftsperson who engineered her own literary survival.
